body: New Zealand bollards have a distinctive red strip wrapping around the top, often with a thin yellow or white reflector on the front or back, unique to the country.
New Zealand uses white licence plates with black text appearing mostly white in blur; some vehicles have custom plates with blue or black sides.
Most poles are concrete with a long single indent running up, often with silver possum guards; circular wooden poles and concrete holey poles exist but are less common.
Give-way signs in New Zealand have a white border with red text, unlike Australia’s black text.
Intersections often feature give-way triangles painted on the road, which are not used in Australia.
Directional and warning signs mostly use white posts; warning signs are diamond-shaped and yellow.
Blue street signs with white text are common in rural New Zealand; other colours appear but blue is most common, unlike Australia.
Roads usually have white outer lines; yellow dashed outer lines appear in populated areas; inner lines are dashed white or double yellow. Australia rarely uses yellow inner lines.
New Zealand uses black-on-yellow chevrons with thin black borders; white on black chevrons are rare. Australia uses similar colours but without borders.
Green directional signs are common; state highway numbers are shown in a red crest. Brown signs indicate landmarks.
Most paved roads have bridge markers; red crests show highway numbers, yellow markers indicate river or bridge names.
Ferns grow commonly in forested areas.
State highways have a sequential numbering pattern north to south, making them easy to find; bollards sometimes display highway numbers.
New Zealand phone numbers consist of seven digits with a two-digit area code; numbers starting with 02 are mobile.
Fonterra farm signs have a regional pattern in their first digit.
Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch have unique bus stop signs.
Cities have distinctive rubbish bins marked with council logos; green lids are rare outside Christchurch.
Waikato and Northland regions have a drier climate and rolling hills, with Northland being especially hilly.
West Coast and parts of Tasman have temperate rainforests and rugged landscapes with many tall hills and mountains.
Southland and Otago have flatter areas with a cold climate and alpine hills, with often stunted vegetation.
The Southern Alps is a large snowy mountain range covering most of the South Island; vegetation lessens farther south.
Hawke’s Bay has dry, golden grassy hills, and features Generation 4 sunny coverage with a white Street View car.
Bright sandy cliffs are common in central Manawatū-Whanganui and parts of Taranaki, Waikato, and a road into Hawke’s Bay.
Northern and southern areas around Queenstown in the Southern Alps have many glacial lakes with teal clear waters.
Mount Taranaki is recognized by its smooth slopes and pointed snowy peak, often visible in flat surrounding areas.
Generation 2 coverage and gravel roads are common in Northland but require other clues for certainty.
Tall hedge and tree rows are characteristic of Canterbury plains; taller hedges are also seen near Tauranga.
Very tall hedges are common in Bay of Plenty, especially around Tauranga.
Vineyards are abundant in Marlborough and Hawke’s Bay but can be found throughout New Zealand.
Corn is predominantly found on the North Island.
New Zealand flax in long, neat rows is mostly seen in Southland.
Marlborough poles often have long square-shaped olive-brown possum guards alongside silver ones.
Many Southland utility poles have long cylindrical silver possum guards, also found sometimes in western Otago.
Holey utility poles are mainly found in Southland and Auckland.
Square concrete poles without indents are common in Southland and also appear in Otago, Taranaki, and Manawatū-Whanganui.
Uneven, off-centre crossbars are found in Otago, Marlborough, Wellington, and Taranaki.
Poles with tall metal bar insulators are seen along the Auckland Waikato border and parts of Waikato.
Some concrete poles in eastern Waikato and Whanganui have white-painted crossbars, also in parts of western Bay of Plenty, Taranaki, Manawatū-Whanganui, and eastern Wellington.
Yellow cow-tag-like tags appear on poles in Gisborne, northern Hawke's Bay, and a few South Island spots.
Warning pole stickers with a yellow triangle between white rectangles are found in Hawke's Bay, northern Waikato, and south of Auckland.
Medium black vertical stickers with 5 digits appear in West Coast, Tasman, southern Canterbury, and southern Northland.
Long black vertical stickers with 6 digits and a small square below occur across North Island (starting with 3 or 4), Southland, and Otago (starting with 8). Variants exist.
Poles near Timaru often have a tall orange painted rectangle warning of live wires.
Small black horizontal pole stickers with numbers are common in Taranaki and Wellington, occasionally in Manawatū-Whanganui, Waikato, and southern Hawke's Bay.
Small white horizontal pole stickers with straight edges occur on several North Island areas; rounded plates are common nationwide.
Solid outer white road lines without middle lines are common in Gisborne, northern Hawke's Bay, and Wellington; Wellington roads tend to be narrower.
Bollards with a green stripe are common in southern Canterbury and some pockets in eastern Southland.
Bollards with a black stripe instead of red are often found in Wellington, especially in older Generation 3 areas.
Wooden fences with tightly packed posts are found mostly on the North Island, northern South Island, and Akaroa.
Wooden fences with wide gaps between posts are common on the South Island and in Taranaki.
Fences with thin metal posts are almost exclusive to the South Island.
Short wooden extensions on fence posts appear often in Hawke's Bay and sometimes Manawatū-Whanganui and Gisborne.
Long wooden fence extensions are mostly in Southland and Hawke's Bay, also visible in Otago.
A car with a white-blue front is mostly found on North Island, occasionally in Canterbury and Marlborough.
A Street View car with a white-blue-white pattern is mostly on the South Island or around and north of Auckland.
Northern New Zealand has many town and city-specific street signs.
Southern New Zealand also has many unique town and city street signs.
The city of Wellington is easily recognized by its hilly terrain.
Stewart Island coverage is limited to the settlement of Oban, noted for a distinct bay full of small boats and only Generation 3 camera coverage.
Tongariro National Park is recognized by low-lying volcanic vegetation, and nearby Mount Ruapehu and Mount Tongariro, often cloud-covered.
Mount Ruapehu roads feature a dark volcanic landscape with sparse vegetation, mainly around Whakapapa Ski Village.
Christchurch roads from 2012 often show earthquake damage like bad road condition, water damage, and missing houses due to 2011 earthquakes.
State Highway 85 in Otago has sections with light snow coverage between Becks and Morisson.
Lower and Upper Hutt lie in a wide green valley running southwest to northeast.
Blenheim is noted for large hill ranges to its north and south.
Fruit farms with green netting are common near Tauranga and Gisborne.
Banks Peninsula (Akaroa) features rocky grassy hills with small tree patches, sometimes including gorse.
Northern Marlborough Sounds is densely forested mountainous terrain protruding into water, mostly covered in Generation 4.
Otago peninsula east of Dunedin combines cabbage trees, yellow-flowered bushes, cone-shaped pines, and New Zealand flax; poles often have off-centre crossbars.
State Highway 73 near Arthur’s Pass has an almost dried-out gravelly riverbed; the Street View car followed a black pickup with two ladders on its roof.
State Highway 94 is characterized by dense red beech forest surrounded by snow-capped mountains.
State Highway 80 in the Southern Alps runs north-south along a glacial valley; west side features snow-capped mountains, east side borders the Tasman River and Lake Pukaki.
Mount Pirongia, a long mountain with two small bumps, and Mount Kakepuku, a volcanic cone to the south, are often viewed together in a flat landscape.
Mount Putauaki in Bay of Plenty has a cut-off top resembling a frog’s head with two big eye-like protrusions.
